A study of the form, content and performance of Agatu songs. PhD thesis, Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria, p. 149.)
catalog_locator: p. 96 (checked against scan), p. 94, sec. 3.1.3 'AGATU' p. 131; Samuel 2015 p. 149.
catalog_quote: In addition, Igede has a four-level, register tone system that seems ancient, since there are no contextual, lexical or grammatical constraints on the occurrence of any of the tones. It would be hard to specify which is the "fourth" tone. All the other Idomoid languages have three-register systems. Except for the very special case of Yala (Ikom), downdrift is rare and downstep non-existent. [p. 96] ... Idoma itself, a cluster of ten dialects strung out from Lafia to Obubra and Ikom, on the Cross River, has Swadesh cognate percentages in excess of 87 percent between its members. These cognations are very obvious; and tonally the cognate forms are at least 98 percent identical in their citation forms, even between the Yala dialects and Otukpo, ... [p. 94] ... 3.1.3 AGATU. The northernmost dialect in old Idoma Division. It borders the south bank of the Benue River and has some communities north of the Benue in Nasarawa. Agatu District and Ochekwu district, speaking a similar dialect, together form the Apa L.G.A. of Benue State. [p. 131] || Samuel 2015: 149: The song is expressed in Agatu, a tonal language which really functions when it is spoken with its proper tone pattern. Despite the fact that its syllables can be indicated by high, mid and low tones, its musical form cannot be satisfactorily rendered in translation.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Agatu is a register tone language with three level tones (high, mid, low); tone, not stress, is the lexically contrastive prosody. No source opened says anything about word stress or accent in Agatu (a full-text search for stress/accent found nothing in Armstrong 1983, Samuel 2015 or Ogra 2017).
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Agatu-specific corroboration: Samuel, Jerry Idu. 2015. A study of the form, content and performance of Agatu songs. PhD thesis, ABU Zaria, p. 149: "The song is expressed in Agatu, a tonal language which really functions when it is spoken with its proper tone pattern. Despite the fact that its syllables can be indicated by high, mid and low tones, its musical form cannot be satisfactorily rendered in translation." (file). Ogra 2017: 37 (citing Odumuh 1994) gives Idoma a three-level discrete register system H/M/L.
new_statements.domain_note: Armstrong's tone remarks concern citation forms of lexical stems in comparative wordlists (Swadesh 200 list from Rev. Hugh Mackay 1963 and Armstrong's own 1951 elicitation from the Chief of Bagaji); word level, no phrase-level prosody discussed. Nothing on stress at any level.
new_statements.identity_note: Agatu is treated by Armstrong (1983: 94, 131) and by Nigerian Idoma scholarship (Abraham's five varieties; Ogra 2017: 5-6, 49) as the northernmost dialect of the Idoma dialect cluster (Idoma = idom1241), not as a separate language; Ethnologue/Glottolog give it its own code agc / agat1236. The quoted Armstrong statement is made for the Idomoid languages as a group (Idoma cluster incl. Agatu, Igede, Akweya, Eloyi, Etulo), with Agatu itself sketched in his sec. 3.1.3; the Agatu-specific tonal statement (H/M/L) is Samuel 2015: 149, a literature PhD by an Agatu-area scholar, not a phonological description.

sources.note: Not about Agatu; nothing on stress. p. 37: Idoma has a three tone-level discrete register system H/M/L (citing Odumuh 1994). pp. 5-6: Agatu is one of Abraham's five Idoma varieties. p. 47: Methodist Mission at Ika studied the Agatu variety in the 1960s (Rev.
